learn: Why recurrence was dropped: the three RNN bottlenecks and the 2017 Transformer
Industry landscape and the three variants (encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder–decoder)
Encoder: embeddings, positional encoding, multi-head attention, position-wise FFN, layer norm, residuals; parameter count ≈12d²
Decoder: masked self-attention, cross-attention, FFN; stack; output layer; parameter count ≈16d²
Vision Transformer: patches, [CLS], learned positions, encoder, classification head; ViT vs CNN
Variants in depth: pretraining objectives (MLM, autoregressive LM, span corruption), use cases, training vs inference
Foundation models; Hugging Face; transfer learning and fine-tuning workflow; metrics; LoRA
intro.why: The Transformer is the architecture behind essentially every modern language, vision and multimodal model. Understanding its blocks, shapes and parameter budget, and how pretrained models are fine-tuned, is the most directly job-relevant material in the course.
prereq: Attention, multi-head attention, masks and positional encoding (Module 8)

sections.title: Recap and what's missing
sections.plain: We have attention types; now we assemble them into an architecture.
sections.body: What we learned (p.4): attention focuses on relevant parts of the input; QKV as information retrieval; self-, multi-head, cross- and masked attention. What's missing: how to organise these mechanisms into a complete architecture; how to handle sequences without recurrence; how to scale to billions of parameters. This module: the Transformer (attention as the only sequence-mixing mechanism) and its three variants.

sections.title: The RNN bottleneck
sections.plain: Sequential, vanishing gradients, fixed memory.
sections.body: RNNs process one token at a time, $h_t=f(h_{t-1},x_t)$, with the hidden state carrying information forward (p.5). Three critical problems: (1) sequential processing: $h_1$ before $h_2$ before $h_3$…, so training can't be parallelised over time (hours → days → weeks); (2) vanishing gradients: early information fades, even LSTM/GRU struggle beyond 100–200 tokens; (3) fixed memory: the hidden state is a bottleneck with limited capacity as sequences grow. Question: can we build sequence models without recurrence?

sections.title: The Transformer solution (2017)
sections.plain: "Attention is all you need": parallel, direct connections.
sections.body:
Key insight (Vaswani et al., 2017, p.6): replace recurrence entirely with self-attention; each token attends directly to all others; no sequential dependency → full parallelisation.

ProblemRNNTransformer
ParallelisationSequentialParallel
Long-range dependenciesVanishing gradientsDirect connections
MemoryFixed hidden stateAttention to all tokens

Impact: 2017 machine-translation breakthrough; 2018 BERT (encoder-only); 2018–2020 GPT series (decoder-only); 2020→ foundation of all large language models; Transformers became the universal architecture for sequences. Scaling (p.7): parallel processing enables massive datasets; direct connections learn complex patterns; flexible architecture adapts to any domain. This led to LLMs (100B+ parameters, trillions of tokens: reasoning, coding, writing), small language models (1B–7B: Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral-7B; on-device, private, low-latency) and specialised models (ViT, CLIP for vision; Whisper, Wav2Vec2 for speech; multimodal models handling text, images and audio). Trade-off: attention costs $O(n^2)$ in sequence length.

sections.title: Real-world applications and industry models
sections.plain: Chat, code, content, science; decoder-only dominates generation.
sections.body:
Applications (p.8): conversational AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini; customer support; assistants); code generation (Copilot, CodeLlama, StarCoder); content creation (writing, summarisation, translation across 100+ languages); scientific research (AlphaFold 3 protein structure prediction, drug discovery).

Observations: decoder-only dominates generative tasks; open models are competitive with proprietary ones; parameter count vs performance is not linear. Note: the providers of GPT-4, Claude and Gemini have not published parameter counts, so those three figures are unofficial estimates (see flags); the open-model sizes are published.

sections.title: Three Transformer architectures
sections.plain: Bidirectional encoder for understanding, causal decoder for generation, both for seq2seq.
sections.body: Why three variants (p.9): different tasks need different information flow; trade-off between understanding and generation; computational efficiency for specific uses. Encoder-only: bidirectional attention → classification. Decoder-only: causal attention → generation. Encoder–decoder: encoder → decoder → seq2seq. Selection: classify or extract → encoder-only; generate text → decoder-only; input and output very different → encoder–decoder.

sections.title: The full architecture; what encoder and decoder do
sections.plain: Encoder builds contextual vectors; decoder generates token by token using them.
sections.body:
Architecture figure (p.12): input embeddings (IE) + positional encodings (PE) of "the cat sat on the mat" feed the encoder block (LayerNorm → multi-head attention → add; LayerNorm → FFN → add), whose output $H_{enc}$ feeds the cross-attention of each decoder block (LayerNorm → masked MHA → add; LayerNorm → cross-attention → add; LayerNorm → FFN → add) over output embeddings (OE) "⟨s⟩ the cat sat on the". The figure uses the pre-norm arrangement (LayerNorm before each sub-layer), as in the equations below; the 2017 paper used post-norm, $\text{LN}(x+\text{Sublayer}(x))$.

Encoder (p.13): transforms the input sequence into rich contextual representations: raw tokens (words, subwords, patches) in, a context-aware embedding per position out. Key capability: bidirectional context: each token attends to all others, capturing relations in both directions (e.g. "bank" in "river bank" vs "bank account"). Multi-head attention lets tokens "communicate"; the FFN lets each token "think" independently; stacking $N$ times builds increasingly abstract representations. Output $H_{enc}\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_{model}}$, used by the decoder (encoder–decoder) or a task head (encoder-only).

Decoder (p.14): generates the output one token at a time: previously generated tokens in (autoregressive), probability distribution over the next token out. Key capability: causal generation: token $t$ attends only to positions $\le t$, so it can't look ahead. Masked self-attention; cross-attention to the encoder (encoder–decoder only); FFN; stacked $N$ times. Output $D_{out}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d_{model}}$; select the next token greedily, by sampling or beam search.

sections.title: Encoder input: token embeddings and positions
sections.plain: X = Embedding(tokens) + PE(positions).
sections.body:
Input embedding (p.16): convert tokens to dense vectors $\mathbf x_i\in\mathbb R^{d_{model}}$ via a learned embedding matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{|V|\times d_{model}}$ (a lookup: row $i$ of $E$ for token id $i$); typical $d_{model}=512$ (base) or 1024 (large). Tokens are usually subwords (WordPiece/BPE), so $|V|\approx$ 30K–50K. (The original paper also multiplies embeddings by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$ and ties input/output embeddings.)

Positional encoding (p.17): attention has no notion of position, so add position information to the embeddings:

$$PE(pos,2i)=\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)\ (1),\qquad PE(pos,2i+1)=\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)\ (2)$$$$X=\text{Embedding}(\text{tokens})+PE(\text{positions})\qquad(3)$$

(p.18) The slide's wording "input embedding concatenate position embedding" contradicts eq. (3): the vectors are added element-wise (same dimension), not concatenated.

sections.title: Encoder: multi-head attention
sections.plain: H heads of size D/H, concatenated and projected by W^O.
sections.body:
Multi-head attention lets each embedding attend to all others; $H$ parallel heads capture different relationships (p.19). For each head $h=1..H$:

$$Q_h=ZW_h^Q,\quad K_h=ZW_h^K,\quad V_h=ZW_h^V\ (4),\qquad \text{head}_h=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q_hK_h^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V_h\ (5),\qquad \text{MHA}(Z)=\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_H)W^O\ (6)$$

Typical: $H=12$ heads, $d_k=d_v=D/H=64$ (BERT-base, $D=768$; the original Transformer used 8 heads of 64 with $D=512$). Cost per layer $O(n^2D+nD^2)$.

sections.title: Encoder: position-wise feed-forward network
sections.plain: Expand ×4, non-linearity, contract; same weights at every position.
sections.body:
$$\text{FFN}(\mathbf x)=\max(0,\mathbf xW_1+\mathbf b_1)W_2+\mathbf b_2,\qquad W_1\in\mathbb R^{D\times4D},\ W_2\in\mathbb R^{4D\times D}$$

The FFN "thinks" independently and processes the information (p.20): a two-layer network that expands $D\to4D$, applies a non-linearity (ReLU; GELU in BERT/ViT), and contracts $4D\to D$, applied independently to each position. Why position-wise: the same weights at each position; adds non-linearity after attention (attention itself is a weighted average, linear in the values); provides capacity for complex transformations: two-thirds of each encoder layer's parameters ($8D^2$ of $12D^2$) sit here. Attention mixes information across positions, the FFN transforms it within each position.

sections.title: Encoder: layer normalisation
sections.plain: Normalise each token's vector across features.
sections.body:
$$\text{LN}(\mathbf x)=\gamma\odot\frac{\mathbf x-\mathbb E[\mathbf x]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}[\mathbf x]+\epsilon}}+\beta\qquad(7)$$

Problem (p.21): training deep networks is hard (vanishing gradients, information loss, unstable optimisation). Solution 1: layer normalisation: normalise across the feature dimension (per token, not across the batch); learnable $\gamma,\beta\in\mathbb R^{d_{model}}$; the same procedure at train and test time, independent of batch size and sequence length (unlike batch norm, see Module 11).

sections.title: Encoder: residual connections and the complete layer
sections.plain: Out = x + Sublayer(x); Z₁ = X + MHA(LN(X)); Z₂ = Z₁ + FFN(LN(Z₁)).
sections.body:
$$\text{Out}=\mathbf x+\text{Sublayer}(\mathbf x)\qquad(8)$$

Solution 2 (p.22): residual (skip) connections, from ResNet: help gradient flow in deep networks ("gradient highways"), easier optimisation, allow very deep models (100+ layers). Complete encoder layer (p.23):

$$Z_1=X+\text{MHA}(\text{LayerNorm}(X))\ (9),\qquad Z_2=Z_1+\text{FFN}(\text{LayerNorm}(Z_1))\ (10)$$
EncoderLayer(X):                     # X: n × D
  Z1 = X  + MHA(LN(X), LN(X), LN(X))  # tokens exchange information
  Z2 = Z1 + FFN(LN(Z1))               # each token transformed separately
  return Z2                           # still n × D

Every sub-layer preserves the $n\times D$ shape, which is what makes the residual additions and stacking possible. Pre-norm (as here) trains more stably for deep stacks; post-norm needs learning-rate warmup.

sections.title: Encoder parameters
sections.plain: ≈ 4d² attention + 8d² FFN = 12d² per layer.
sections.body:
Each token is embedded into a $d_{model}$-dimensional vector and sequences up to $n_{max}$ tokens are processed (p.24): $|V|$ 30K–50K; $d_{model}$ 512 (base) or 1024 (large); $n_{max}$ 512–2048.

ComponentParameters
Input embedding$|V|\times d_{model}$
Positional encoding$n_{max}\times d_{model}$ (if learnable; 0 if sinusoidal)
Layer norm (2 per layer)$2\times2\times d_{model}=4d_{model}$
Multi-head attention$4\times d_{model}^2$ ($W^Q,W^K,W^V,W^O$)
Feed-forward$2\times d_{model}\times d_{ff}=8d_{model}^2$ with $d_{ff}=4d_{model}$
Total per layer$4d_{model}+4d_{model}^2+8d_{model}^2\approx12d_{model}^2$

Biases are omitted. Check (code ex1): $d=768$ gives 7.08M per layer; with biases, 12 layers plus embeddings ($|V|=30{,}522$, $n_{max}=512$) ≈ 108.9M, matching BERT-base's published ≈110M.

sections.title: Encoder stack
sections.plain: N identical layers: 6 (original), 12 (BERT-base), 24 (BERT-large).
sections.body:
$$H^{(\ell)}=\text{EncoderLayer}^{(\ell)}(H^{(\ell-1)}),\ \ \ell=1,\dots,N,\qquad H^{(0)}=\text{InputEmbedding}+\text{PositionalEncoding}\qquad(11)$$

Stack of $N$ identical layers (identical in shape, each with its own weights) (p.25): original Transformer $N=6$; BERT-base 12; BERT-large 24; GPT-3 96 (decoder, same principle). Output $H^{(N)}\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_{model}}$: a rich contextual representation for each input token; each position has attended to all other positions $N$ times; passed to the decoder via cross-attention in encoder–decoder models.

sections.title: Decoder layer: masked attention and cross-attention
sections.plain: Z₁ = Y + MaskedMHA, Z₂ = Z₁ + CrossAttn(·, H_enc), Z₃ = Z₂ + FFN.
sections.body:
$$Z_1=Y+\text{MaskedMHA}(\text{LN}(Y))\ (12),\qquad Z_2=Z_1+\text{CrossAttn}(\text{LN}(Z_1),H_{enc})\ (13),\qquad Z_3=Z_2+\text{FFN}(\text{LN}(Z_2))\ (14)$$

where $H_{enc}$ is the encoder output (p.27). Masked multi-head attention (p.28): self-attention with causal masking: token $t$ attends only to positions $\le t$. Why: match training and inference; at inference we generate one token at a time, so training must simulate this autoregressive process.

$$\text{mask}_{ij}=\begin{cases}0&i\ge j\\-\infty&iCross-attention (encoder–decoder attention, p.29): the decoder attends to the encoder output: query from the decoder layer, keys and values from $H_{enc}$; no masking (all source tokens visible). Why needed: connect source and target, letting the decoder focus on relevant source positions.

$$\text{CrossAttn}(Q_{dec},K_{enc},V_{enc})=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q_{dec}K_{enc}^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V_{enc},\quad Q_{dec}=\text{LN}(Z_1)W^Q,\ K_{enc}=H_{enc}W^K,\ V_{enc}=H_{enc}W^V$$

The attention matrix is $m\times n$ (target × source). Code ex1 checks that changing a later target token leaves earlier decoder outputs unchanged (causality).

sections.title: Decoder parameters
sections.plain: ≈ 16d² per layer: 33% more than an encoder layer.
sections.body:
Component (p.30)Parameters
Output embedding$|V|\times d_{model}$
Positional encoding$n_{max}\times d_{model}$ (learnable)
Layer norm (3)$3\times2\times d_{model}=6d_{model}$
Masked MHA$4d_{model}^2$
Cross-attention$4d_{model}^2$
Feed-forward$8d_{model}^2$
Total per layer$6d_{model}+8d_{model}^2+8d_{model}^2\approx16d_{model}^2$

Same vocabulary and dimensions as the encoder. The decoder layer has 33% more parameters than an encoder layer (16 vs 12 $d_{model}^2$). A decoder-only model (GPT) has no cross-attention, so its layers are ≈12$d^2$ like encoder layers.

sections.title: Decoder stack and output layer
sections.plain: N layers of 3 sub-layers; then Linear → softmax over the vocabulary.
sections.body:
$$D^{(\ell)}=\text{DecoderLayer}^{(\ell)}(D^{(\ell-1)},H_{enc}),\ \ \ell=1..N,\qquad D^{(0)}=\text{OutputEmbedding}+\text{PositionalEncoding}\qquad(17)$$

(p.31) Original Transformer $N=6$; each layer has 3 sub-layers (vs 2 in the encoder): masked self-attention, cross-attention, FFN. Output $D^{(N)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d_{model}}$: each position has attended to previous positions $N$ times (masked) and to all encoder positions $N$ times. Every decoder layer receives the final encoder output $H_{enc}$.

$$\text{logits}=D^{(N)}W_{out}+b_{out},\ W_{out}\in\mathbb R^{d_{model}\times|V|}\ (18),\qquad P(y_t\mid y_{(p.32) Flow: $\mathbb R^{d_{model}}\xrightarrow{\text{linear}}\mathbb R^{|V|}\xrightarrow{\text{softmax}}$ probabilities $\xrightarrow{\text{token selection}}y_t$, by greedy, sampling (temperature, top-k, top-p) or beam search. $W_{out}$ is often tied to the embedding matrix.

sections.title: From NLP to vision: why ViTs work
sections.plain: Treat an image as a sequence of patches.
sections.body:
Traditional CNNs (p.34): convolutions extract local features, pooling builds spatial hierarchy, inductive bias of translation equivariance and locality. The ViT innovation (2020): treat an image as a sequence of patches; apply a pure Transformer (no convolutions); learn visual relationships through self-attention. Key insight: CNNs hard-code locality through kernels; ViTs learn relationships between all patches; trade-off: need more data, but more flexible. ViTs excel with large-scale pretraining (ImageNet-21K, JFT-300M) and transfer learning.

What ViT does (p.35): image classification with a pure Transformer; encoder-only; image → class probabilities. Divide the image into fixed-size patches (16×16), flatten each and project linearly, add positional encoding, process through the encoder; prepend a [CLS] token whose output feeds an MLP head. Why it works: self-attention captures spatial relationships globally from the first layer.

sections.title: ViT architecture, patch embedding and [CLS]
sections.plain: 196 patches of 16×16×3 → 768-d vectors, plus [CLS], plus learned positions.
sections.body:
Architecture (p.36): encoder-only (image in, class probabilities out); a learnable [CLS] token is prepended to the patch sequence, aggregates global information via self-attention, and its final representation is used for classification. Flow: image → patches → encoder → [CLS] → class.

Image to patches (p.37): $I\in\mathbb R^{H\times W\times C}$ (e.g. 224×224×3), $N$ patches of $P\times P$ (typically $P=16$): $N=\frac{H\times W}{P^2}=\frac{224\times224}{16\times16}=196$. Linear projection:

$$\mathbf z_i=\text{Flatten}(\text{patch}_i)\,W_p,\qquad W_p\in\mathbb R^{(P^2\cdot C)\times d}\qquad(20)$$

Flatten: 16×16×3 = 768 numbers; project to $d$ (typically 768); $Z=[\mathbf z_1;\dots;\mathbf z_N]\in\mathbb R^{N\times d}$. Prepend $\mathbf z_{[CLS]}\in\mathbb R^d$: final sequence $[\mathbf z_{[CLS]};\mathbf z_1;\dots;\mathbf z_N]\in\mathbb R^{(N+1)\times d}$. (A $P\times P$ convolution with stride $P$ is exactly this projection.)

Positional encoding (p.38): self-attention is permutation-invariant (equivariant, Module 8), so patch positions need explicit encoding. ViT uses learnable embeddings $E_{pos}\in\mathbb R^{(N+1)\times d}$ (197 positions: [CLS] at 0 + 196 patches), learned during training; 1-D embeddings suffice, no 2-D structure hard-coded:

$$\mathbf z_0^{(0)}=[\mathbf z_{[CLS]};\mathbf z_1;\dots;\mathbf z_N]+E_{pos}\in\mathbb R^{(N+1)\times d}\qquad(21)$$

sections.title: ViT encoder and classification head
sections.plain: Standard encoder layers (GELU FFN); LN([CLS]) → linear → softmax.
sections.body:
$$\mathbf z_1^{(\ell)}=\mathbf z_0^{(\ell-1)}+\text{MHA}(\text{LN}(\mathbf z_0^{(\ell-1)}))\ (22),\qquad \mathbf z_2^{(\ell)}=\mathbf z_1^{(\ell)}+\text{FFN}(\text{LN}(\mathbf z_1^{(\ell)}))\ (23),\qquad \text{FFN}(\mathbf x)=\text{GELU}(\mathbf xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2\ (24)$$

(p.39) Same as the Transformer encoder: LayerNorm → MHA → add → LayerNorm → FFN → add, stacked $L$ times (ViT-Base $L=12$, $H=12$ heads, $d_k=d/H=64$, $W_1\in\mathbb R^{d\times4d}$). Each patch (including [CLS]) attends to all other patches, capturing global spatial relationships.

Output (p.40): after $L$ layers $\mathbf z_2^{(L)}\in\mathbb R^{(N+1)\times d}$; extract $\mathbf z_{[CLS]}^{(L)}\in\mathbb R^d$, which aggregates information from the entire image.

$$\mathbf h=\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf z_{[CLS]}^{(L)})\ (25),\qquad \text{logits}=\mathbf hW_{head}+b_{head},\ W_{head}\in\mathbb R^{d\times K}\ (26),\qquad P(y=k\mid I)=\mathrm{softmax}(\text{logits})_k\ (27)$$

Final prediction $\hat y=\arg\max_kP(y=k\mid I)$; training with cross-entropy. Cost: attention over $N+1=197$ tokens is $197^2\approx38.8$K scores per head per layer; halving $P$ quadruples $N$ and multiplies attention cost by ≈16.

sections.title: ViT vs CNNs
sections.plain: CNNs: strong bias, data-efficient. ViT: weak bias, scales and transfers.
sections.body:
AspectCNNsViT
Inductive biasStrong (locality, translation equivariance)Weak (learns from data)
Data efficiencyGood with small datasetsRequires large-scale pretraining
ScalabilityLimited by kernel sizeScales well with model size
Global contextLimited (small receptive field early)Excellent (self-attention)
ComputeEfficient convolutionsQuadratic in sequence length
Transfer learningGoodExcellent

Guidelines (p.41): CNNs for small datasets (<100K images) and limited compute; ViT when large-scale pretraining and transfer learning are available; hybrid: a CNN stem with a Transformer body. (Data-efficient variants such as DeiT, and hierarchical ViTs like Swin, narrow the gap.)

sections.title: Why three variants? Comparison
sections.plain: The attention pattern decides the variant.
sections.body:
AspectEncoder-onlyDecoder-onlyEncoder–decoder
AttentionBidirectionalCausal (masked)Both
Information flowAll tokens see allToken sees only pastEncoder bidirectional, decoder causal
Task typeUnderstandingGenerationTransformation
Use caseFull context neededSequential outputInput ≠ output
EfficiencySingle pass, parallelSimpler, scalableMost flexible, compute-intensive

(p.43) Different tasks need different architectures: not all NLP tasks require generation, not all need bidirectional context; trade-offs between capability and efficiency. Key design decision: the attention pattern.

sections.title: Encoder-only (BERT family)
sections.plain: Bidirectional; pretrained with masked language modelling.
sections.body: Architecture (p.44): only the encoder stack; bidirectional self-attention; output a contextual representation per token. Pretraining: masked language modelling (MLM): randomly mask 15% of input tokens and predict them from context in both directions ("The [MASK] sat on the mat" → "cat"). (BERT replaces 80% of selected tokens by [MASK], 10% by random tokens, 10% unchanged, and originally added next-sentence prediction.) Use cases: text classification (sentiment, spam); named-entity recognition; extractive question answering (answer spans); sentence embeddings (similarity, clustering). Figure (p.45): "Teddy was US President" → IE + PE → encoder ($N\times$ bidirectional MHA + FFN) → task head → [PER, O, LOC, O]. Popular models: BERT (2018, 110M–340M), RoBERTa (2019, optimised BERT training), DistilBERT (2019, 40% smaller, 60% faster).

sections.title: Decoder-only (GPT family)
sections.plain: Causal; pretrained to predict the next token.
sections.body: Architecture (p.46): only the decoder stack (no encoder, hence no cross-attention); causal self-attention (token $t$ attends to $\le t$); output a distribution over the next token. Pretraining: autoregressive language modelling: predict the next token given previous ones, maximising $\prod_tP(x_t\mid x_{

sections.title: Encoder–decoder (T5, BART)
sections.plain: Bidirectional encoder + causal decoder with cross-attention.
sections.body: Architecture (p.48): both stacks; encoder bidirectional over the input; decoder causal self-attention + cross-attention to the encoder. Pretraining objectives vary: T5 casts every task as text-to-text (span corruption: mask spans, generate them); BART is a denoising autoencoder (corrupt and reconstruct); mT5 is multilingual text-to-text. Use cases: machine translation, summarisation, question answering (question + context → answer), data-to-text. Figure (p.49): "this book" → encoder → $H_{enc}$ → decoder over "⟨s⟩ yeh kitab" → $P(y_t\mid y_{

sections.title: Training vs inference: examples
sections.plain: Training is parallel with teacher forcing; generation is one token at a time.
sections.body: Encoder–decoder (translation) (p.50): training input "this book is good" → target "yeh kitab acchi hai"; the decoder sees all target tokens with masking and predicts all tokens in parallel (teacher forcing). Inference: step 1 [⟨start⟩] → "yeh"; step 2 [⟨start⟩, "yeh"] → "kitab"; and so on. Encoder-only (NER): "Teddy is a soft toy" → [O, O, O, O, O]; "Teddy was US President" → [PER, O, LOC, O]: the entire sentence is processed at once with bidirectional context (and context disambiguates "Teddy"). Decoder-only (completion): prompt "The weather today is" → "sunny and warm with a gentle breeze", each token generated from all previous ones. Inference caches past keys and values (KV cache) so each new token costs $O(n)$ attention rather than recomputing the prefix.

sections.title: When to use what
sections.plain: Classify/extract → encoder; generate → decoder; transform → encoder–decoder.
sections.body:
AspectEncoder-onlyDecoder-onlyEncoder–decoder
AttentionBidirectionalCausalBoth
TasksClassification, NER, QAChat, completionTranslation, summary
ExamplesSentiment, entity taggingCode generation, dialogueEnglish→Hindi, abstractive summarisation
ModelsBERT, RoBERTaGPT-4, Claude, LLaMAT5, BART, mT5
ContextFull sentenceLeft to rightSource full, target causal
SpeedFast (parallel)Slow (sequential generation)Medium

Selection guide (p.51): need to classify or extract → encoder-only; need to generate text → decoder-only; input language ≠ output language → encoder–decoder. In practice, large decoder-only models now handle many "encoder" and "seq2seq" tasks by prompting, at higher inference cost.

sections.title: Large-scale pretraining and foundation models
sections.plain: Self-supervised pretraining on huge text, then adapt.
sections.body:
Why pretrain (p.52): learn general language understanding from massive unlabelled data; transfer to downstream tasks with limited labelled data; better than training from scratch. Objectives by architecture: encoder-only MLM (BERT, RoBERTa); decoder-only autoregressive LM (GPT, LLaMA); encoder–decoder span corruption/denoising (T5, BART). Fine-tuning approaches: full fine-tuning (all parameters); parameter-efficient (LoRA, adapters: <1% of parameters); prompting (zero-/few-shot, no parameter updates).

Foundation models landscape (p.53): proprietary (GPT-4, Claude 4, Gemini 3): API access only, highest performance, closed weights. Open source (LLaMA 3, Mistral, BERT): full control, self-hosting, fine-tuning, research. Trade-offs: proprietary = best performance, no control, API costs; open = full control, hosting costs, requires expertise. (Several "open" LLMs are open-weights under custom licences rather than open source in the OSI sense.)

sections.title: Hugging Face Hub
sections.plain: An open hub of pretrained models, datasets and the transformers library.
sections.body: What is Hugging Face (p.55): an open platform for ML models, datasets and applications; 500,000+ pretrained models (more today); the easy-to-use transformers Python library; community-driven. Popular checkpoints: encoder-only bert-base-uncased, roberta-large, distilbert-base; decoder-only gpt2, meta-llama/Llama-3-8B, mistralai/Mistral-7B; encoder–decoder t5-base, facebook/bart-large, google/flan-t5-large. Benefits: instant access, no pretraining needed, proven performance. Always use the checkpoint's own tokenizer (AutoTokenizer) and check its licence.

sections.title: Transfer learning and the fine-tuning workflow
sections.plain: Pretrain (self-supervised, TB of text) → fine-tune (1K–100K labelled examples).
sections.body:
Paradigm (p.56): pretraining on a large unlabelled corpus (TB of text; self-supervised MLM or autoregressive) → pretrained model → fine-tuning on task-specific data (1K–100K examples; supervised: classification, NER, …) → task-specific model. Why not train from scratch: it needs massive data (billions of tokens) and expensive compute (thousands of GPU-hours); pretrained models already learned general language patterns.

Workflow (p.57): (1) load the pretrained model; (2) prepare task data: tokenise with the pretrained tokenizer, create train/validation splits, prepare labels; (3) fine-tune with a small learning rate (typical $2\times10^{-5}$ to $5\times10^{-5}$), few epochs (2–5, to avoid overfitting), Adam with weight decay (AdamW); (4) evaluate on validation: monitor accuracy, F1, loss; early stopping if validation degrades.

sections.title: Fine-tuning example: IMDb sentiment
sections.plain: AutoTokenizer + AutoModelForSequenceClassification + Trainer.
sections.body: Task (p.58): classify movie reviews as positive/negative; dataset IMDb (25K train, 25K test); base model BERT or RoBERTa. Steps shown on the slides: load AutoTokenizer and AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased', num_labels=2); tokenise with padding to max_length, truncation, max_length=512, using dataset.map(..., batched=True). Training (p.59): TrainingArguments(output_dir='./results', num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=16, per_device_eval_batch_size=64, learning_rate=2e-5, weight_decay=0.01, evaluation_strategy='epoch', save_strategy='epoch', load_best_model_at_end=True); Trainer(model, args, train_dataset, eval_dataset); trainer.train(); trainer.evaluate() and print accuracy. As written, the slides' evaluation would not report eval_accuracy unless a compute_metrics function is passed, and recent library versions rename evaluation_strategy to eval_strategy; code ex3 shows a completed version (not executed here: it needs the libraries, a download and ideally a GPU).

sections.title: Best practices and evaluation metrics
sections.plain: Small LR, freezing strategies, 2–5 epochs, clipping; task-appropriate metrics.
sections.body:
Best practices (p.60): learning rate $2\times10^{-5}$–$5\times10^{-5}$; layer freezing: full fine-tuning (best performance), gradual unfreezing (top layers first), freeze embeddings (update only task layers); batch size 16–32; epochs 2–5 (more → overfitting risk); weight decay 0.01–0.1; gradient clipping max norm 1.0; at least ≈1,000 labelled examples, more (10K–100K) is better. Warmup (e.g. 6–10% of steps) is also standard.

Metrics (p.61): classification: accuracy, F1, confusion matrix; NER: entity-level F1 (precision/recall on full entities), token-level accuracy; QA: exact match (EM), token-overlap F1; generation: BLEU (precision-based, translation), ROUGE (recall-based, summarisation), perplexity (how well the model predicts text, $\exp$ of mean token cross-entropy).

sections.title: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: LoRA
sections.plain: Freeze W; learn ΔW = BA with rank r ≪ d.
sections.body:
Problem (p.62): full fine-tuning updates all parameters (BERT-base 110M), memory and compute intensive. LoRA (low-rank adaptation): freeze pretrained weights; add trainable low-rank matrices $\Delta W=BA$ with $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$, $A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d}$, $r\ll d$; update <1% of parameters:

$$W_{new}=W_{frozen}+\alpha\cdot BA\qquad(28)$$

Benefits: 10–100× fewer trainable parameters; lower memory footprint (no optimiser state for frozen weights); faster training; comparable or better performance. Details: $B$ is initialised to zero so training starts at the pretrained model; the scale is usually $\alpha/r$; after training $BA$ can be merged into $W$, so inference costs nothing extra; one base model can host many small task adapters. Arithmetic (code ex2): a 768×768 matrix has 589,824 weights vs 12,288 for $r=8$ (2.1%); adapting $W_Q$ and $W_V$ in all 12 BERT-base layers trains 294,912 parameters (≈0.27%). QLoRA combines LoRA with a 4-bit quantised frozen base.

sections.title: Summary and emerging trends
sections.plain: Pure attention, three variants, pretrained models, efficient fine-tuning.
sections.body: What we learned (p.63): Transformers revolutionised AI through pure attention; three architectures (encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder–decoder); the foundation of modern LLMs and multimodal models; Hugging Face makes pretrained models accessible; fine-tuning adapts them efficiently. Emerging trends: multimodal Transformers (text + image + audio); efficiency (sparse attention, linear attention, LoRA); long context (100K–1M token windows); mixture of experts (sparse activation). Practical takeaway: start with pretrained models, fine-tune on your task data, use parameter-efficient methods for large models.

sections.title: Further comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
Post-norm (2017 paper)Pre-norm (slides, GPT-2+)
Formula$\text{LN}(x+F(x))$$x+F(\text{LN}(x))$
Deep stacksNeeds careful warmupTrains stably
Final LayerNormBuilt inAdd one after the stack
  • "Transformers have no recurrence, so generation is parallel." Training is parallel; autoregressive generation is still one token at a time.
  • "Encoder-only models can't be used for generation at all." They're not designed for left-to-right generation, but BERT-style models fill in masks; generation needs a decoder.
  • "More parameters always win." Data quality, training tokens (e.g. compute-optimal scaling), and fine-tuning matter as much.
  • "LoRA reduces inference cost." It reduces training memory; merged inference costs the same as the base model.
  • "[CLS] is special because of its position." It's just a learned token; it becomes a summary because the head is trained on it.

code.title: Transformer encoder and decoder layers from scratch
code.explain: Pre-norm encoder layer (eqs 9–10) and decoder layer (eqs 12–14) with multi-head, masked and cross-attention; a causality check; per-layer parameter counts (≈12d² and ≈16d²) and a BERT-base total (≈109M).
mistakes: Forgetting the causal mask in the decoder (the model learns to copy the next token).
Feeding the encoder's per-layer outputs to cross-attention instead of the final H_enc.
code.notes: In PyTorch: nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model, nhead, dim_feedforward, norm_first=True, batch_first=True).
code.code:
# A pre-norm Transformer encoder layer and decoder layer from scratch, plus the session's parameter counts (NumPy)
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def softmax(Z): Z = Z - Z.max(-1, keepdims=True); E = np.exp(Z); return E / E.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
def layer_norm(X, g, b, eps=1e-5): mu = X.mean(-1, keepdims=True); var = X.var(-1, keepdims=True); return g * (X - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + b
def mha(Xq, Xkv, P, H, mask=None):
    n, D = Xq.shape; dk = D // H
    Q, K, V = Xq @ P["WQ"], Xkv @ P["WK"], Xkv @ P["WV"]
    heads = []
    for h in range(H):
        s = slice(h * dk, (h + 1) * dk); S = Q[:, s] @ K[:, s].T / np.sqrt(dk)
        if mask is not None: S = np.where(mask, S, -np.inf)
        heads.append(softmax(S) @ V[:, s])
    return np.concatenate(heads, 1) @ P["WO"]
def params(D, dff):
    P = {k: rng.normal(0, D ** -0.5, (D, D)) for k in ("WQ", "WK", "WV", "WO")}
    P.update(W1=rng.normal(0, D ** -0.5, (D, dff)), b1=np.zeros(dff), W2=rng.normal(0, dff ** -0.5, (dff, D)), b2=np.zeros(D))
    return P
relu = lambda x: np.maximum(0, x)
def encoder_layer(X, P, H):                       # eqs (9)-(10): Z1 = X + MHA(LN(X)); Z2 = Z1 + FFN(LN(Z1))
    g, b = np.ones(X.shape[1]), np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    Z1 = X + mha(layer_norm(X, g, b), layer_norm(X, g, b), P, H)
    return Z1 + relu(layer_norm(Z1, g, b) @ P["W1"] + P["b1"]) @ P["W2"] + P["b2"]
def decoder_layer(Y, Henc, P, Pc, H):              # eqs (12)-(14): masked self-attn, cross-attn, FFN
    g, b = np.ones(Y.shape[1]), np.zeros(Y.shape[1]); m = Y.shape[0]
    Z1 = Y + mha(layer_norm(Y, g, b), layer_norm(Y, g, b), P, H, np.tril(np.ones((m, m), bool)))
    Z2 = Z1 + mha(layer_norm(Z1, g, b), Henc, Pc, H)
    return Z2 + relu(layer_norm(Z2, g, b) @ P["W1"] + P["b1"]) @ P["W2"] + P["b2"]
D, H, n, m = 16, 4, 6, 5
X = rng.normal(size=(n, D)); Henc = X
for l in range(2): Henc = encoder_layer(Henc, params(D, 4 * D), H)
print("encoder output H_enc shape", Henc.shape)
Y = rng.normal(size=(m, D)); Dout = decoder_layer(Y, Henc, params(D, 4 * D), params(D, 4 * D), H)
print("decoder output shape", Dout.shape)
# causality check: changing a later target token must not change earlier decoder outputs
Y2 = Y.copy(); Y2[-1] += 10; rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
P1, P2 = params(D, 4 * D), params(D, 4 * D); a = decoder_layer(Y, Henc, P1, P2, H); b_ = decoder_layer(Y2, Henc, P1, P2, H)
print("earlier positions unchanged when the last target token changes:", np.allclose(a[:-1], b_[:-1]))
# parameter counts (weights only, as on the slides)
for d in (512, 768, 1024):
    enc = 4 * d * d + 2 * d * 4 * d + 2 * 2 * d; dec = 8 * d * d + 2 * d * 4 * d + 3 * 2 * d
    print(f"d_model={d}: encoder layer {enc:,} (~12 d^2 = {12*d*d:,}), decoder layer {dec:,} (~16 d^2 = {16*d*d:,})")
d = 768; V = 30522; n_max = 512
enc_layer = 4*d*d + 4*d + 2*(d*3072) + 3072 + d + 4*d     # with biases and 2 LayerNorms
emb = V*d + n_max*d + 2*d + 2*d
print(f"BERT-base estimate: 12 layers x {enc_layer:,} + embeddings {emb:,} = {12*enc_layer + emb:,} (published ~110M)")

code.title: ViT patching and LoRA arithmetic
code.explain: Splits a 224×224×3 image into 196 patches of 768 numbers, builds z₀ with [CLS] and positions, and computes LoRA's trainable fraction.
mistakes: Reshaping patches without transposing (mixes pixels from different patches).
code.notes: timm / Hugging Face ViTForImageClassification; peft.LoraConfig(r=8, target_modules=['query','value']).
code.code:
# Vision Transformer patching and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) arithmetic (NumPy)
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
H = W = 224; C = 3; P = 16; d = 768
N = (H * W) // (P * P); print(f"patches N = {H}*{W}/{P}^2 = {N}; sequence with [CLS] = {N + 1}; flattened patch = {P*P*C}")
img = rng.random((H, W, C))
patches = img.reshape(H // P, P, W // P, P, C).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4).reshape(N, P * P * C)
Wp = rng.normal(0, 0.02, (P * P * C, d)); Z = patches @ Wp
cls = rng.normal(0, 0.02, (1, d)); Epos = rng.normal(0, 0.02, (N + 1, d)); Z0 = np.vstack([cls, Z]) + Epos
print("z_0 shape", Z0.shape, "; patch-projection parameters", Wp.size + d)
print(f"self-attention matrix per head: {N+1} x {N+1} = {(N+1)**2:,} entries; with 32x32 patches: {(H*W)//(32*32) + 1}^2 = {((H*W)//(32*32)+1)**2:,}")
# LoRA: W_new = W_frozen + alpha * B A with B: d x r, A: r x d
for r in (4, 8, 16):
    full = d * d; lora = 2 * d * r
    print(f"one {d}x{d} matrix: full {full:,} vs LoRA r={r}: {lora:,} ({100*lora/full:.2f}%)")
L = 12; per_layer_qv = 2 * 2 * d * 8; print(f"BERT-base LoRA r=8 on W_Q and W_V in all {L} layers: {L*per_layer_qv:,} trainable of ~110M ({100*L*per_layer_qv/110e6:.2f}%)")
# low-rank update is exact when the true change is low rank
dW = rng.normal(size=(d, 4)) @ rng.normal(size=(4, d)); U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(dW)
print("rank of a d x d update built as B(d x 4) A(4 x d):", int((s > 1e-8).sum()))
B0 = np.zeros((d, 8)); A0 = rng.normal(0, 0.01, (8, d)); print("LoRA starts at the pretrained model (B = 0 => BA = 0):", np.allclose(B0 @ A0, 0))

code.title: Fine-tuning BERT on IMDb with Hugging Face
code.explain: The slides' Trainer example completed with an accuracy metric, dynamic padding, warmup and clipping. Not executed in this build (needs the libraries, model download and a GPU), so no output is shown.
mistakes: Calling trainer.evaluate() without compute_metrics and expecting eval_accuracy.
Using a learning rate like 1e-3: destroys pretrained features.
code.notes: A 3-epoch run on one modern GPU takes tens of minutes; expect ≈93–94% IMDb accuracy for bert-base (typical published range).
code.code:
# Fine-tuning BERT for IMDb sentiment with Hugging Face (the session's example, completed).
# Needs: pip install transformers datasets evaluate accelerate torch ; a GPU is strongly recommended.
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, TrainingArguments, Trainer
import numpy as np, evaluate

ds = load_dataset("imdb")                                  # 25k train / 25k test reviews
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased", num_labels=2)

def tokenize(batch):
    return tok(batch["text"], truncation=True, max_length=256)  # 512 is the model maximum; 256 trains ~2x faster
train = ds["train"].shuffle(seed=42).map(tokenize, batched=True)
val = ds["test"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(5000)).map(tokenize, batched=True)

acc = evaluate.load("accuracy")
def compute_metrics(p):
    return acc.compute(predictions=np.argmax(p.predictions, -1), references=p.label_ids)

args = TrainingArguments(output_dir="./results", num_train_epochs=3, learning_rate=2e-5, weight_decay=0.01,
                         per_device_train_batch_size=16, per_device_eval_batch_size=64, warmup_ratio=0.06,
                         eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch", load_best_model_at_end=True,
                         max_grad_norm=1.0, fp16=True)
trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train, eval_dataset=val,
                  tokenizer=tok, compute_metrics=compute_metrics)   # tokenizer enables dynamic padding
trainer.train()
print(trainer.evaluate())
